nodes.question: How does injection molding exchange tooling investment for repeatable plastic parts?
nodes.observed: Molten thermoplastic is forced into a cooled, shaped mold and ejected after solidification. The source emphasizes expensive engineered tooling, short repeat cycles and high volumes of near-identical parts.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: A permanent tool encodes geometry into every cycle. Mold filling, cooling and ejection impose design constraints: wall thickness variation produces unequal cooling and warpage; draft and accessible parting/ejection paths affect whether a geometry can be released.
nodes.failure_to_intervention: Sharp corners, nonuniform walls and insufficient draft concentrate stress or impede ejection. The source recommends early tooling collaboration, suitable draft, and more uniform wall thickness rather than treating these as post-production defects.
nodes.transferable_insight: Production scale changes the optimal geometry and investment: the mold amortizes over many parts, while hard-to-eject geometry increases tooling complexity.
unresolved_questions: At which quantity does a specific tool design beat printing or CNC alternatives once tooling, scrap and revision risk are included?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Choose a plastic enclosure; compare designs for mold parting/draft and a printed alternative. Obtain a tooling estimate or real quotation rather than assuming a break-even quantity.

nodes.question: Why can expendable sand molds create large, internally complex metal parts?
nodes.observed: A sand mold forms a cavity for poured metal; it is broken apart to release the casting. Sand casting supports ferrous and nonferrous alloys, large parts, and lower-volume production, typically followed by surface finishing or machining.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The mold does not need to survive extraction, unlike a reusable die. That frees some internal geometries and part sizes but transfers burden to patternmaking, melt flow, solidification, shrinkage allowances and finishing.
nodes.failure_to_intervention: Changes in wall section and cooling rate can produce distortion or defects. The source recommends considering draft, gradual transitions, fillets, gating and material shrinkage during design rather than only after casting.
nodes.transferable_insight: Tool reusability is one independent manufacturing variable: expendable tooling broadens accessible geometry and volume regimes, even while increasing per-part preparation.
unresolved_questions: When do surface finish, porosity and machining costs eliminate the apparent savings of an expendable mold?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Trace a real casting from part drawing through pattern, mold, casting, machining and inspection; identify which geometry and tolerance requirements must be deferred to later operations.

nodes.question: What do layer-building processes gain and sacrifice by avoiding a custom mold?
nodes.observed: The process survey describes stereolithography and selective laser sintering among layer-based rapid prototyping methods. CAD geometry is sliced and formed incrementally from resin or powder; it notes no custom mold tooling, rapid design iteration, and surface/finishing limitations.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Machine-controlled deposition or solidification substitutes a digital toolpath for a custom shape-defining physical tool. Supports, residual material and surface steps differ across processes: in the book's SLS description unsintered powder surrounds the part, while SLA uses built support structures.
nodes.transferable_insight: Removing per-shape hard tooling accelerates variation and prototyping, but does not remove material, machine, support, accuracy or post-processing constraints.
unresolved_questions: Which process becomes favorable when functional part properties—not simply shape similarity—matter?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Take a real complex part with an internal cavity. Compare SLA, powder-bed printing and a split-and-joined approach, including support removal and inspection access.

nodes.question: Why can waterjet cutting reach materials that heat-based cutting may damage?
nodes.observed: A high-pressure pure-water or abrasive jet removes material along a programmed profile. The source emphasizes cold cutting without a heat-affected zone, low tooling cost, and increasing cut drag and taper in deeper or harder material.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Erosion by a directed jet avoids a thermally melted cutting edge. Cut quality and speed still depend on thickness, hardness, abrasive, nozzle motion and part support; the stream can lag as depth increases.
nodes.failure_to_intervention: The source's glass-disc case uses wedges during cutting and polishing afterward. It demonstrates that part support and finishing remain necessary even when no shaped die is required.
nodes.transferable_insight: A process's main physical side effect (heat, force, contamination, residual stress) may matter more than its nominal ability to cut a shape.

source_sections.section: Water Jet Cutting and glass-disc case

unresolved_questions: For an actual part, how does abrasive-waterjet edge accuracy and time compare to laser cutting, punching and machining?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Specify the same sheet-metal or glass profile for waterjet and one alternative process. Obtain toolpath time/kerf estimates and measure edge quality of real samples.

nodes.question: How can reorienting and splitting an FFM part change strength, time and reliability?
nodes.observed: Smyth's four dimensionally equivalent cylinder models take 38, about 12, just under 12, and 20 minutes respectively, with 2.53, 3.13, 2.99, and 3.58 g of filament. They differ in support, surface, strength expectations and assembly.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Layer-by-layer extrusion creates direction-dependent strength, especially across layer interfaces. Orientation changes how loads cross layers and how much support or bed contact is needed. Splitting a part replaces difficult print geometry with easier prints plus a joining step.
nodes.failure_to_intervention: An upright narrow cylinder risks adhesion instability; horizontal printing can damage undersides or require support. Printing two halves or designing interlocking subparts can avoid unsupported geometry at the expense of joints.
nodes.transferable_insight: Geometric equivalence does not imply manufacturing equivalence. Shape decomposition and process orientation are design variables, not mere machine settings.

source_sections.section: Anisotropy; print orientation/design refactoring; support; layer fusion

unresolved_questions: Does the predicted strength ranking hold for a given polymer and printer?
When do joint weaknesses outweigh the printing gains from decomposition?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Print two equal-function designs with differing orientations or split geometry. Record failed attempts, total time including assembly, mass, dimensional error and load direction; destructively test multiple specimens rather than accept the book's example as a universal rule.

nodes.question: How do tolerances turn an ideal CAD shape into a manufacturable assembly?
nodes.observed: Shigley chapter 20 describes GD&T as defining allowed variation in size, position, orientation and form so that design, manufacturing and quality inspection share a usable geometric specification. Smyth chapter V emphasizes calibration and over-extrusion compensation for printed mating features.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: CAD nominal geometry is only the target. Real parts vary, and assemblies fail when positional/form deviations combine even if individual dimensions seem acceptable. GD&T establishes datums and admissible geometric variation; printing offsets should reflect measured machine behavior.
nodes.transferable_insight: A manufacturing process is useful only if its tolerance distribution can satisfy an assembly's functional contract. Nominal resolution alone does not establish usable fit or interchangeability.
unresolved_questions: Which actual feature deviations dominate assembly failure for an accessible 3D printer?
Which tolerances can be verified with calipers versus more involved metrology?
nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Design mating printed features with nominal clearances; print a dimensioned variation matrix, measure real dimensions, identify fit failure thresholds and distinguish slicer compensation from a model's geometric allowances.

nodes.question: How can we synthesize a physical mechanism from desired motion, force, and constraints?
nodes.why: A mechanism's function is not identical to its geometry: the same movement may be realized by links and joints, a shaped cam, a flexible member or another arrangement. Inputs, degrees of freedom, load paths, actuation and constraints determine useful alternatives.

nodes.question: How can we manufacture reliable products at a specified quantity, quality, and cost?
nodes.why: A prototype that works once is not a production route. Tooling reuse, cycle time, yield, inspections, revision costs, assembly and operating volume can reverse which process is economical.

nodes.question: Which mechanism topologies create the motion, force, or dwell we want?
nodes.why: A desired output behavior can admit linkage, cam, gear, Geneva, ratchet or flexural realizations. Compare their motion and force laws, constraints and loads before choosing physical parts.

nodes.question: When does a mechanism concept survive materials, flexure strain, fabrication, and assembly?
nodes.why: A mechanism with correct idealized motion may still break, jam, fatigue or fail tolerances. Kinematics, structural compliance and manufacturing limits are coupled.

nodes.question: When should shape be encoded in reusable tooling, expendable tooling, or digital instructions?
nodes.why: Mold reuse, destructible patterns and programmable toolpaths lead to different setup, revision and per-unit costs; feasible material and shape constraints must be screened first.

nodes.question: How do mechanical advantage and motion ratios constrain a mechanism's output?
nodes.observed: Sclater's mechanical fundamentals distinguish greater output force from greater output energy: obtaining more force requires less displacement, and friction consumes useful work.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: At a chosen operating point, a mechanism transforms input displacement, velocity and force. Ideal work balance couples force multiplication to reduced travel; nonideal friction and geometry-dependent ratios further limit performance. A designer must specify output motion and force together, not independently.
nodes.transferable_insight: Start mechanism design with an input-output contract (force, travel, speed, timing, load), then filter linkages, gears or screws for physically plausible ratios and efficiency. A gear ratio is not a free gain in both speed and torque.

source_sections.section: Ch. 1: efficiency, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, levers and linkages

nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Using a real lever or screw-jack specimen, measure applied travel and force against output travel and force; estimate work efficiency and compare the measured result to a frictionless model.
unresolved_questions: Which specific linkage geometries meet a stated force/travel envelope under practical backlash and friction?

nodes.question: How can continuous rotation produce an intermittent output with controlled dwell?
nodes.observed: Sclater's Geneva examples show a driver entering an output wheel slot to index it and disengaging while the wheel stays stationary. Modified drives use cam-shaped radial motion or gear variants to change acceleration, speed profile and dwell.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: A Geneva couples and uncouples motion periodically: the driver applies displacement during a short engagement, while locking/dwell geometry holds the output between indexes. Its acceleration spikes and entry/exit loads become design constraints; changing the driver trajectory changes those loads without changing the required indexing function.
nodes.transferable_insight: Specify an output timeline (move, settle, hold) before choosing a cam, ratchet or Geneva. Identical net indexing does not imply identical acceleration, duty cycle, wear or control cost.

source_sections.section: Ch. 7: Twenty Geneva Drives and modified Geneva drives

nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Compare a Geneva wheel with a cam-controlled or stepper-driven indexing alternative for the same step angle and cycle rate; measure dwell accuracy, peak acceleration and repeatability.
unresolved_questions: At what cycle speed do dynamic loads overwhelm the simplicity of the mechanical dwell?

nodes.question: When should elastic deformation replace pin joints or articulated rigid links?
nodes.observed: Howell distinguishes stiffness (resistance to deflection) from strength (resistance to failure), and demonstrates rigid-body replacement: identify the desired motion of a linkage, then replace selected joints or links with elastic members. The handbook's four-bar synthesis generates 28 compliant configurations before selecting based on load and strain.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: A flexure creates controlled relative motion through material strain rather than sliding or rolling contact. Removing joints can reduce assembly and play, but stores elastic energy and introduces stress, fatigue, stiffness and limited-motion constraints. The most favorable topology depends on what must move, what must remain stiff and the direction of load.
nodes.failure_to_intervention: Simply replacing all joints with thin flexures can sacrifice load capacity. In the bicycle-derailleur study, the authors retain several rigid links and pin joints while evaluating two compliant alternatives instead of maximizing compliance blindly.
nodes.transferable_insight: A mechanism can be simultaneously flexible in intended directions and strong against failure. Distinguish degrees of freedom, desired stiffness, strength, strain limits and fatigue life before deciding whether to use conventional joints or flexures.

source_sections.section: Ch. 1: Stiffness and strength; flexible yet strong
Ch. 8: Rigid-body replacement and bicycle derailleur case

nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Design a small repeatedly actuated clamp as (A) pinned links and (B) a compliant substitute. Compare required force, travel, off-axis motion, assembly steps, measured strain/fatigue and print orientation.
unresolved_questions: Which material and fabrication route meets the desired fatigue life and precision?
How well does a simplified flexural model predict the real build?

nodes.question: How can desired degrees of freedom generate candidate flexure architectures?
nodes.observed: Howell's freedom and constraint topology (FACT) procedure specifies desired degrees of freedom, identifies a corresponding freedom space, chooses nonredundant constraints from the complementary space, and optionally adds redundant constraints for stiffness, load capacity or symmetry. A ball-joint probe example uses three intersecting independent rotational degrees of freedom.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The designer chooses allowable motions first, rather than copying an existing mechanism's geometry. Complementary constraints forbid unwanted motions; alternative physical arrangements can realize the same kinematic freedom. Redundancy may improve load behavior but changes stress and stiffness.
nodes.transferable_insight: Represent motion requirements as allowed and forbidden degrees of freedom before choosing specific beams or joints. This produces a family of mechanically different candidates with equivalent nominal motion.

source_sections.section: Ch. 6: freedom/constraint spaces and FACT synthesis

nodes.minimum_reconstruction_probe: Choose a precision platform allowed to translate in X and Y but resist Z translation and unwanted rotations. Identify target freedoms, propose two alternative constraint topologies, then verify their actual parasitic motion.
unresolved_questions: How do nominally equivalent constraint arrangements differ in off-axis stiffness and real manufacturing error?

cross_book_insights.claim: A CAD shape is not a sufficient manufacturing design.
cross_book_insights.reason: Process choice determines supports, release, shrinkage, load direction and finishing; tolerancing determines whether resulting parts assemble.

cross_book_insights.claim: Part decomposition is an operator over manufacturing feasibility.
cross_book_insights.reason: A split FFM cylinder can print faster with better support behavior, but adds joins and fitted interfaces; similar tradeoffs arise when casting/finishing components separately.
cross_book_insights.status: cross-process hypothesis illustrated by sources, not universal quantitative rule

cross_book_insights.claim: Tooling reuse, not just process name, changes which production volumes are economical.
cross_book_insights.reason: Injection molding encodes reusable cavities; sand casting consumes mold; layer-build and waterjet paths are digitally revised. Actual break-even quantities require price and throughput measurements.
cross_book_insights.status: supported conceptual contrast; no measured break-even

cross_book_insights.claim: A mechanism's function has multiple physical realizations.
cross_book_insights.reason: Rigid components convert travel and force; flexures allow similar intended freedoms by controlled strain. Load capacity, friction, assembly and lifetime distinguish alternatives.
cross_book_insights.status: mechanism synthesis supported by inspected chapters; performance ranking remains conditional

cross_book_insights.claim: Mechanism synthesis and manufacturing selection cannot be completed independently.
cross_book_insights.reason: The flexure geometry that supplies intended motion must survive anisotropic material properties, feasible orientation, tolerances and real operating cycles.
cross_book_insights.status: cross-book engineering synthesis; requires component-specific validation

cross_book_insights.claim: A single category tree is not a reliable model of the mechanism landscape.
cross_book_insights.reason: Howell's own mechanism catalog observes overlapping classifications because kinematics and force–deflection functions coexist; one design participates in several useful classification questions.
cross_book_insights.status: explicit catalog limitation, Ch. 10; motivates several goal-conditioned navigation trees

competence_probe.title: One functional bracket, three manufacturing routes
competence_probe.task: Specify a bracket with loads, holes, clearance, and a real mounting use. Compare (A) a printed monolithic bracket, (B) printed pieces with fasteners, (C) a waterjet-cut plate plus joining/finishing. Use a fourth process only if it changes the decision.
competence_probe.decision: Select the process/assembly that satisfies the functional tolerances at lowest total cost for a stated quantity; diagnose rather than explain away failed samples.

navigation_principle.canonical_items: Research observations, studies, case nodes and source anchors are recorded once with stable IDs.
navigation_principle.multiple_views: Different big-picture purposes activate overlapping canonical items with different parent relationships. A view is an inquiry-specific path, not a claim of unique natural classification.
navigation_principle.boundary: No attempt is made to turn every TOC entry into a separate question; a new item earns its place when it changes an alternative, a failure mode, a source path or a practical capability.
